doc.title: Frank Wess — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

title: Macular degeneration and writing music with help
summary: Wess discusses his failing vision, fruitless doctor visits, and having others write out his arrangements.

story.theme_name: Illness, injury and the deaths of colleagues
story.community_name: Illness, injury and death among jazz musicians

blocks.x: You know, and one thing that is certainly affecting your life in recent years, is your vision.
Oh, well my health, you know, that’s age. We don’t want to get into that. That could be an organ recital. (Laughs) We don’t have time for that one.
Can I ask you, is it macular degeneration?

Yeah, yeah but I’ve been to doctors, and doctors, and doctors and they all shine a bright light in my eyes and blind me and then they say, “I’m sorry, we can’t help you. Be sure to see the lady on the way out.” What can you do, they just don’t have anything. I’ve heard of a stem cell program they have in Cologne, Germany but nobody seems to think too much of it, and it’s expensive, and there aren’t any guarantees of anything.
Has that affected, you know, your process of communicating?
Well, it affects your income because I can’t read any music. I can’t…I haven’t read a paper in two years. I just can’t see it, but at the same time I can pick up a stray pin off the floor.
I can see a stray pin and reach down and pick it up. But, I mean, I can’t read music, or words, or papers. It’s laborious. This, magnifying the field, is so small, it’s hard to read.
I would imagine that would affect any kind of writing of music.

Yeah, well I have to have somebody, I have to tell them what I want to right. Usually I have people that understand. Dennis Mackrel has done two things for me, for this next gig, and Anita Brown has done a couple of things too. I just explain to them what I have in mind and they know, pretty well, what to do.
